learn.title: The name of an array
learn.body: In most expressions, an array's name turns into the address of its first item. So with `int a[3]`, writing `a` gives the same address as `&a[0]`. That is why you can store an array name in a pointer: `int *p = a;`.

learn.title: Two ways to reach an item
learn.body: This prints `10 20 30`, then 1, then 99. `p[2]` is the third item, and `*(p + 1)` is the second. `a[1] == *(a + 1)` is true: square brackets are just a shorthand for this.

learn.title: Same thing
learn.body: With the array above, what are `a[2]` and `*(a + 2)`?
steps: `a + 2` is the address two items after the start

learn.title: Arrays in functions
learn.body: When you pass an array to a function, the function receives only a pointer to its first item. Inside the function, `sizeof` gives the size of a pointer, 8 bytes here, not the array. So pass the length as a second argument.
`p` and `a` can both reach the same bytes. Writing `p[0] = 99` changed `a[0]`, because there is only one array.

questions.prompt: With `int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};` and `int *p = a;`, what is `*(p + 1)`?
questions.explanation: `p + 1` points at the second item, which holds 20.

questions.prompt: With `int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};` and `int *p = a;`, what is `p[2]`?

questions.explanation: `p` points at the array's first item, so the write changes the array.

questions.prompt: In most expressions, an array name becomes a \_\_ to its first item.
questions.explanation: The array name decays to a pointer to its first element.

questions.prompt: A function receives `int a[]`. What does `sizeof a` give inside it?
choices: The size of the whole array
questions.explanation: The parameter is really a pointer, so you must pass the length separately.
Add 3 items to the address, then dereference it.

questions.prompt: Match each expression to the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Brackets and pointer arithmetic describe the same positions.
